slides.title: Geometry on Surfaces
slides.notes: Open by naming the chapter's central shift: geometry is no longer only a model space, but a surface that may be curved, glued, or quotient-built. The lecture should keep local measurement and global topology in conversation. Ask students to listen for three recurring diagnostics: circle growth, boundary identifications, and Euler characteristic.

slides.title: Three Measurements, One Story
slides.notes: Use this roadmap to prevent the lecture from feeling like a catalog. Circle growth detects the sign and scale of curvature near an observer. Polygon words encode topological bookkeeping. Gauss-Bonnet explains why those two languages are not independent by converting total curvature into Euler characteristic.

slides.title: Curvature From Circle Growth
slides.notes: Treat the image as an experimental instrument. In flat geometry the circumference grows as two pi r. Positive curvature makes circles fall short, while negative curvature makes them grow too quickly. The key point is local: an inhabitant can estimate curvature without seeing the whole surface, using only radius and circumference measurements.

slides.title: Scaled Model Spaces
slides.notes: This slide introduces the unified notation X sub k without making students memorize three unrelated geometries. The sign of k chooses the family, while the magnitude sets the ruler. Emphasize that rescaling lengths changes numerical curvature, so comparisons across models need a consistent curvature scale.

slides.title: Parallelism Still Remembers Curvature
slides.notes: The angle of parallelism is a useful bridge back to the hyperbolic chapter. It shows that distance from a line controls the limiting angle of a nonintersecting geodesic. Students should notice that this is not a Euclidean phenomenon with a fixed parallel direction; it is a curvature-dependent measurement.

slides.title: From Polygons To Surfaces
slides.notes: Move slowly through the boundary word idea. A polygon is not the surface yet; it is an instruction sheet for gluing. Once edges are paired with orientations, vertices merge into equivalence classes, and the counts of vertices, edges, and faces produce Euler characteristic. This is topology made computable.

slides.title: Orientability And Euler Characteristic
slides.notes: Use the classifier as a dashboard rather than a black box. Orientability records whether local orientation survives every gluing cycle. Euler characteristic compresses vertex, edge, and face bookkeeping into one invariant. The classification theorem then says that compact connected surfaces are organized by orientability and genus or crosscap number.

slides.title: Gauss-Bonnet As A Conversion Rate
slides.notes: Frame Gauss-Bonnet as the chapter's exchange rate between analysis and topology. The integral of Gaussian curvature plus boundary turning terms equals two pi times Euler characteristic. For closed constant-curvature surfaces, the equation becomes especially sharp: area, curvature sign, and topology constrain one another.

slides.title: Which Topologies Accept Which Curvatures
slides.notes: This is the moment to connect the map to examples. The sphere has positive Euler characteristic and fits positive curvature. The torus has zero Euler characteristic and admits a flat quotient model. Higher genus surfaces have negative Euler characteristic, so constant negative curvature becomes the natural uniform geometry.

slides.title: Quotients Make Surfaces From Space
slides.notes: The quotient construction turns a model geometry into a surface by declaring points equivalent under a group of isometries. Stress the clean action condition: if the group has fixed points or pathological accumulation, the quotient may fail to be a smooth surface. Good quotient geometry depends on the group action, not just the model space.

slides.title: Dirichlet Domains Are Local Maps
slides.notes: A Dirichlet domain is the region closer to a chosen basepoint than to any of its translated images. It is a practical way for an inhabitant to draw a fundamental domain from distance comparisons. The bisectors encode which copies of the basepoint become neighbors after quotienting.

slides.title: Instructor Board Work
slides.notes: This board-work slide is meant to be done live, not solved in advance. Choose a simple boundary word, count the identified vertices, paired edges, and polygon face, then compute Euler characteristic. The value is not the arithmetic alone; students see how a gluing instruction turns into a topological invariant.

slides.title: Common Misreadings
slides.notes: Use these warnings to separate model drawings from intrinsic claims. A flat-looking polygon can encode a curved or multiply connected surface after gluing. A quotient by any group is not automatically a manifold. Finally, curvature sign is local, while Euler characteristic is global; Gauss-Bonnet links them through an integral, not by making them identical.

slides.title: Computational Lab
slides.notes: Close by pointing students toward the notebook as a reproducible laboratory. The artifacts are not decorations: each one corresponds to a measurement or invariant that can be checked. Encourage students to vary curvature scale, change a boundary word, and move the Dirichlet basepoint, then explain which quantities change and which remain invariant.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: End with the three diagnostics again so the lecture has a memorable shape. Curvature can be measured by how circles grow. Topology can be encoded by polygon gluing data. Quotient and Dirichlet domains show how local copies assemble into a surface. Gauss-Bonnet is the bridge tying those observations together.
